The AAW Symposium is in Portland Oregon next
year, May23-26. AAW Symposiums are a big deal!
This symposium only gets close to us once every six
years. And it’s returning to Portland because it was
one of the best attended six years ago. If you’ve
never been, it is well worth the time and expense
to attend a symposium. You will come away with a
wealth of knowledge and inspiration. If you have
been, you can hardly wait for the next one. Six
years ago we had about 25 members attend and
several brought along their spouses. If you are sure
you are going, it is good to book your hotel early. I
suggest you read all about it at https://
www.aawsymposium.org/
I’d like to welcome all of the new members that
have joined. One oddity this year is that we have
payments from a half dozen people, but we have
no registration info from them. We do not know
who they are! If per chance you are not receiving
emails from the Guild, please contact president@gvwg.ca – we’ll get things sorted out.
The President’s Challenge for January is “baseless”.
Think of something that typically has a flat base and
see what happens to the object when it orients itself on its centre of gravity.
Steve

These pieces were inspired by trying new things
with spheres. People at work said it reminded
them of eyeballs so on one of them I formed a
spherical iris shape and painted the inside to enhance the eyeball experience. It is held in place by
a piece of foam and can be easily removed. I liked
the offset and the veining texture and have since
the original made quite a few of these. This particular one was done as a demo piece for the Prince
George Woodturning symposium this fall. Once I
have brought it to the guild for the Instant Gallery I
will ship it to Prince George for them to auction it
or whatever they choose. This one is made from
Catalpa, a beautiful and aromatic wood, and has a
diameter of 4.50".

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
The topic for October’s Focus on Fundamentals
meeting was working alone in the shop. In my own
workplace we have a working alone policy. As
much as possible we do not schedule people to
work alone and, in the rare event that it occurs,
there is a procedure to check on that person at
least once an hour for as long as they are working
alone. As woodturners, most of us work alone in
our shops at home and it seemed like an interesting idea to hear what people do to mitigate the
hazard of working alone.
This meeting was a little different since we did not
have a main presenter. The topic was introduced
and various people in the meeting chimed in with
their thoughts on the topic. The result was a lively,
wide-ranging discussion that covered a variety of
safety topics that can be broadly broken down into
a few different categories.
•
Safe work practices
•
Safe equipment
•
How to get help
•
Being prepared if something goes wrong
Steve Daechel kicked things off by making the point
that statistics show that we are far more likely to
be injured in our own shops than we are in the
workplace. From there he proceeded to give us a
number of safety considerations that fell into these
categories and other people chimed in. I’ll try to
summarize below without going into who said
what.
Safe Work Practices
•
Be in the right mindset. If you are tired, distracted or unfocused these are the times that
accidents are most likely to occur. Taking
breaks to cleanup near the end of the day not
only leads to a safer work setting but gives you
an opportunity to rest and assess if you still
have the energy to work safely.
•
Build safety into your work process rather than
treating it as an add-on.
•
Keep PPE close to where you work so it is convenient to put it on and make using it a habit.
•
Understand the tools you are using and how to
use them safely.
•
A chainsaw is a regularly used tool by many
turners that is often used in too casual a manner.
 Use chaps and face shield.
 Understand how kickback happens, watch
out for the tip of the saw so it doesn't contact anything.
 Get training (this article is far too short to
be comprehensive on chainsaw safety and I
am no expert)
•
Think through what you are going to do before
you do it. A two second job that you don’t think
through all the way is more likely to result in
injury than a larger job that is well planned.
•
Think about your hand position and where your
hands are going to go if something goes wrong.
•
When using a chuck on the lathe adopt the
habit of always keeping a hand on the key
when it is in the chuck. It can be thrown dangerously if it is forgotten or if the lathe is somehow turned on with the key in the chuck.
•
If doing pyrography, or any other burning, it
was noted that it should not be done at the end
of the day or just before leaving the shop. Fires
can develop hours after the work has finished.
•
If working on a ladder be careful not to overreach. Some people use the belt buckle rule
that your belt buckle should stay within the
frame of the ladder, others believe in not
(Continued on page 5)

November 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
letting their hips go outside the ladder frame.
•
On a bandsaw several suggestions were made:
 Set the blade guard to a height appropriate
for the workpiece that does not expose
more of the blade than necessary.
 A two-inch no-go area for hands around the
blade was suggested.
 Do not work on the side of the saw. If the
blade breaks this is the danger area. It is
much safer to stand at the front.
•
If other people enter the shop don’t make assumptions about their skills or knowledge.
Teach those who do enter regularly how to get
your attention in a safe manner that won’t distract you at a critical moment.
Equipment Safety
•
If using a table saw check the setup before using it. Make sure that the fence is square and
use a push stick.
•
Push sticks should be made from plywood and
not solid wood. Solid wood is more prone to
sudden breakage that could cause an accident.
•
If you are having to force wood through the cut
on a bandsaw, the blade is likely dull and an
accident is more likely to occur. Stop and sharpen or replace the blade. This is something that
can also be applied to table saws, turning tools
and anything else we might be using that needs
to be sharp to work properly. A dull tool is a
dangerous tool!
•
Deenergize tools before doing maintenance or
changing blades, bits, etc. If it is a corded tool
you can unplug it. If it is battery operated remove the battery.
•
A grinder can build up enough metal shavings
to become a fire hazard, particularly if a magnet is used to collect them. Regularly cleaning
up around the sharpening station to keep them
from building up is advisable.
How to get help
•
It’s a good idea to have someone who knows
where you are and what you are doing who will
check in periodically.
•
Have a phone available in the workshop.
•
Having Alexis or one of the other personal assistants that come with electronic devices can
be used to dial 911 for you in an emergency.
•
A fall detection device that some seniors have
could be an option. It was noted that some
smartwatches have this feature and the details
likely vary between brands and models. One
caution is that you could find yourself accidentally calling 911 if you are not careful.
Being prepared if something goes wrong
•
Have a first aid kit in the shop. Some training in
how to use it is helpful as well.
•
An eyewash station could be useful. There are
models that come with bottled rinse water and
can be mounted on the wall so plumbing is not
a requirement.
•
A fire extinguisher kept next to the shop exit.
I have undoubtedly missed some of the topics that
were discussed. The video is available on our private YouTube channel and worth a watch. There
were lots of good reminders for anyone and a few
tips that were new for myself. While the discussion
included many topics that I would hope people follow whether they are alone or have others people
in their shop safety takes on an added importance
when there may not be help immediately available.
I hope that everyone reading this comes away with
a few lessons or reminders. Stay safe and keep
turning!
(Continued from page 4)

When moving from the older incandescent task
lamps for your lathe to using the new more efficient LED lamps you must consider the fuzz you can
incur if you chose the wrong lamp type.
Many LED spot lamps use the cheaper multi source
style emitters for cost reduction as in these photos:
What you see are several points of light coming
from each lamp.
Now add a fast rotating piece of wood on your
lathe and you get multiple points of light that your
eye is trying to focus on. Your eye can not handle
all these inputs at the same time. This can blur
your focus on your cutting tool and the spot where
you are trying to see how your cut is going.
What you really need is a single source emitter
lamp like these photos:
These lamps give your eye one source of light like
the old incandescent and halogen lamps gave you
with out the heat. They are not easy to find and
you really have to pay attention to the details
when buying.
Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

Following on the heals of taking an in-person class
with Elizabeth Weber during her tour with the
FVWG, I am still very much energized creatively
and hungry for even more.
Currently traveling, while possible, is a much bigger
challenge and while my calendar often gets filled
up, here is my top 5 people that I would do my best
to clear the calendar and immerse myself like a
sponge to see what I might soak up from them.
I fully recognize that not all of these artists may be
available as the demands on their time and energy
are significant and simply not possible. But a girl
can dream, so here is my list and a quick summary
of why.
Top pick…Derek Weidman
https://www.instagram.com/derek_weidman_sculptor/
https://vimeo.com/273303320
https://www.woodturner.org/

Derek’s multi-axis sculpting a dragon’s head is a
demonstration I have now easily have seen a couple dozen of times. As he walked through his process, there were so many ideas, warnings, and suggestions he made that got tucked into my turning
and makers toolbox. I am so curious too of him
using the chainsaw for sculpting and his mind simply works in so many curious ways that would open
my world to even more possibilities. I know Dustin
Cook has formed a friendship with this creative
soul while attending some AAW Symposiums, so
fingers crossed, this just might be possible.
And the others…in no particular order because I
would love to learn from them all!
Eli Avisera
https://en.eliavisera.com/
https://www.instagram.com/eli_avisera/
This woodturner has visited the GVWG before. I
knew nothing about him until I purchased the very
last blank out of Art Leistman’s collection and
found myself on a journey of discovery that I was
simply blown away by. How did he make that
blank? How do I get my hands on more of his
blanks…because this skill and attention to detail is
likely way out of my league…and besides, I have
yet to explore segmented turning…but Eli Avisera,
along with Colin Delory, might get me to have the
inspiration to dive right in. Unfortunately, given
the tragedy that is currently happening in and
around his homeland of and area of Jerusalem, his
attention is likely focused on other matters. But if
he could travel to this area, I’d love to help make it
happen.
Paul Russell
https://www.instagram.com/paulrusselldesigns_/
I have it on very good authority that Paul is a really
fun guy to learn creative woodturning from. My
WIT Exchange 2024 partner is the President of the
Guild where Paul is a member of the board. Emily
was helping Paul film a demonstration for the
Woodturners Worldwide Online Symposium and,
knowing of the kinds of things I love to explore,
made sure I took the time to watch Paul’s demo.
Emily knows me well and ever since I saw Paul turn
the branch wood into a vessel I have been wanting
to learn even more. But he is a reserved guy, too,
who has yet to hit the road as a demonstrator.
Ruby Cler
https://rubycler.com/
https://www.instagram.com/ruby.cler/
I first saw some of Ruby’s work during the show
and tell with Pat Carrol’s Meet the Woodturner.
Since that time, Ruby has become a regular guest
and participate within the Record Power Live
Demonstrations community. Ruby has been turn-
(Continued on page 8)

November 2023

Page 8
ing since 1972 and has seen and been inspired by
many influential turners such at Stuart Mortimer,
Alan Batty, and so many more. Her maple Spiral
vase, influenced by Stuart’s work, has me curiously
exploring my own twists and forms. Ruby has traveled to so many places and worked with so many
turners that I love that she is one person, who lives
in Canada, that could bring a culmination of all
those influences as we dive in and play together.
And since first writing this paragraph, Ruby has
now been interviewed by Pat Carroll on Meet the
Woodturner and I want to learn from her even
more, especially how she does the secret compartment sphere boxes, to see her homemade Rose
Engine/ Guilloche she uses for making patterns and
textures on pendants, and her work on doing a
Celtic knot inlay for pen turning to name but a few.
Michael Hosaluk
https://michaelhosaluk.com/
https://www.instagram.com/michaelhosaluk/
Another turner that has visited GVWG before and
that we hear so many of our members fondly speak
of the influence he had on their own creative process. Michael loved to play, explore, and push the
boundaries of form. He is one of those turners
who managed to find a style that is all his own so
that if anyone in the turning community comes
across his work, they can correctly identify that it is
the work of Michael Hosaluk. So how does he feel
about being an inspiration to other turners? Does
he enjoy others trying to emulate and copy his
work? What is his process and how does he take
something simple and small and translate it into
something larger and with its own voice?
Michael has had some family challenges these past
few years and understandably is lost in a fog of
what comes next for him. When or as he emerges,
here is someone that I’d love to explore and play
with shape, form, finish and more with him leading
the creative process.
The next best thing, if these people listed above
are not able to fit a trip to the Vancouver area into
their busy and challenging lives, then there are various other options that I’d be keen on too, like an
IRD (Interactive Remote Demo), a slide show
presentation and conversations, probably via
zoom, and until then, I’ll continue to follow their
journey on Instagram and be inspired by their
work.
And just maybe, as I step into a new role for the
GVWG, some of my visions that have been brewing
in my head are another step closer coming to life.
And although I have said it before, I will say it
again, I have very deep respect, appreciation, and
gratitude for everyone who have been part of my
journey into the world of woodturning. I’m simply
having so much fun! You? Who would you like to
learn from?

sym·po·si·um (noun)
a conference or meeting to discuss a particular
subject.
a collection of essays or papers on a particular
subject by a number of contributors.
a drinking party or convivial discussion, especially as held in ancient Greece after a banquet
Each year for the last 32 years the American Association of Woodturners has held a “symposium”
where people who love woodturning gather together to share and enjoy. As we prepare for the
event this year in Portland, OR many are taking advantage of it being close by to attend for the first
time. To help folks appreciate all that happens at
these events we formed a discussion panel to talk
about the event and to answer questions. The panel was made up of Art Liestman (frequent presenter at AAW), Bruce Campbell (AAW panelist 2009),
Ed Pretty (Presenter this year), and Larry Stevenson
(regular attendee).
The annual symposium takes place is a different
city each year roughly following a pattern of East,
Central, East, Central, West of the continental USA
and this roughly corresponds to the distribution of
the membership of the AAW.
The Rotations
The core of the event is the “rotations”. These are
90-minute demonstrations or discussions and as
many as 11 are happening at the same time with
four session on Friday and Saturday, and three on
Sunday. Fortunately, most presentations are given
more than once so if you want to see two things at
are scheduled the same time you can up the second at another time.
You do not need to “reserve” or “book” a space for
these events. They are on a first-some-first-serve
basis but the more popular events can be very full.
It is not possible to see all the presentations and
you may find yourself in something that is not what
you expected. It is OK to quietly leave or even drop
in for a few minutes and then move on.
The Instant Gallery
One of the truly outstanding parts of the AAW is
the Instant Gallery. This is just like our club event
except that each attendee may put in three (3)
items. With as many as 2,000 attendees there
could be up to 6,000 pieces on display but
“usually” there are 1,500-2,000 items. Just simply
walking through the room is inspirational and it can
take a number of hours to give it the time it deserves.
Picture taking is allowed normally but if there is a
NO PHOTOS sign please be respectful. And the best
part is that you might see and get to talk to the
maker.
The Trade Show
All the manufactures and vendors of woodturning
gear strive to attend this show. Over 70 companies
have already booked for this year and you see
many of the products that you have seen in magazines or on the internet. You can also talk to lots of
talented and informative representatives in the
booths.
Thursday Night (Opening Remarks and Special
Interest Presentations)
Opening remarks for event take place Thursday
night at 6:30. Afterwards there are a Number of
session dedicated to special topics like pen turning,
segmented work, ornamental turning, gadgets and
gizmoos, Women in Turning and so on. This year,

long-time turner Christian Burchard will give a talk

Volunteer Opportunities
There are a range of volunteer opportunities that
can help to enrich your visit. These include being a
gallery volunteer to the two special exhibitions or
the instant gallery, being a room volunteer for one
or more rotations, working in the Tool Room, helping with the hands-on classes, and so on.
Networking and Recharging
The symposium is a great way to meet people and
exchange ideas. It is also a place to recharge your
creative energies and fill your brain with new ideas.
Whether in the Instant Gallery, at a booth in the
Trade Show, or simply over lunch, opportunities to
network are everywhere.
Fund-raising Events
We all know about Beads of Courage thanks to the
work that Brian Lunt has been doing. If you make a
box you can deliver it at the Symposium
You can donate a bow to the Portland-area “Empty
Bowl” project. Art mentioned that you should
watch this sales table because special “Easter Eggs”
can appear – like bowls made by famous turners.
It can be a chance to pick up a “name” piece for a
song.
Finally, if you have a few tools lying around that
you never use, consider donating them to the AAW
Tool Bank. They will be given to selected chapters,
educators, and non-profit groups for the purpose
of teaching the art and craft of woodturning to
youth and under-represented groups.
Social Hour and Live Auction
On Friday afternoon there is a social hour (4:30 –
5:30) followed by the ever-popular Live Auction. At
this event, live and on-line bidding takes place on
museum-quality work at the AAW Live Benefit Auction. It is fun to watch the action or bid yourself.
Funds raised will be used by the AAW to develop
and deliver woodturning education and service
programs for our member community worldwide.
Special Exhibitions & Auctions
There are several juried exhibitions at each symposium. Any AAW member may apply to these shows
and those that are selected have their work on display, appear in the show catalog and, optionally,
have their work sold at a live or silent auction.
The AAW’s Professional Outreach Program (POP)
2018 juried exhibition is Out of the Woods. The
works will showcase a mix of imaginative and individual interpretations of the theme, ranging from
wryly humorous to highly personal.
Dia•Log is the juried Member Exhibition this year
reflecting the city of Portland’s and the state’s long
logging history. The exhibition will showcase a wide
range of interpretations, from philosophical to
down-to-earth.
AAW Silent Benefit Auction - Participate in the
slower pace of silent bidding on a variety of turned
works and other items. Funds raised will be used
by the AAW to continue to develop and deliver
woodturning education and service programs for
our member community worldwide.
Instant Gallery Critique and Intimate Critiques
Sunday at 11:00 there will be a panel critique of
selected pieces from the instant gallery. This is a
great chance to hear world-class artists discuss the
pieces they have selected and why they feel each
piece stands out. If you want a critique of one of
your pieces you may sign up for an “Intimate Critique”. Here you can discuss your work with
Conclusion
To summarize, there are a LOT of things happening
over the 3½ days of the symposium and as with
most wood turning events people are just as curious and willing to share as you are. And, as with
most things, the more you get back.

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I got into woodworking during 2020 after watching
too many videos on the internet and picking up
some cedar roots off the side of the road in my
neighbourhood. I spent a few months messing
around with DIY projects and ‘restoring’ (read-
butchering) old hand tools. Eventually, an old Rockwell Beaver lathe came up for free on Facebook
Marketplace and I jumped on it. After a little fixing
up, I did a bit of turning (scraping and burning) for
Christmas presents. It was fun but I had no idea
what I was doing. Still, I decided to jump on a midi
lathe during a KMS Black Friday ‘sale’ and keep at
it. I suppose I should’ve known that I was already
hooked at that point; haha. I’d quit my low-level
finance job a few months before and was looking
for a way to make money on my own terms. Seeing
how much I enjoyed woodworking and woodturning, I decided that I’d take a shot at a business in it.
I knew that I was severely lacking in the skills needed to make that business a reality, so I went look-
(Continued on page 12)
I really like turning wood. It fills me with a sense of happiness and balance that I’d been without for a large
part of my life.

November 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
ing for education to remedy that. I eventually
found the GVWG and decided to join, hoping that I
could find mentorship and education on woodturning. I took a Turning 101 class with Ed Pretty, Cathy
Friesen and Peter Hill and it completely changed
my turning. Over time, I’ve come to find that on
top of being a great educational resource, the guild
is a wonderful community that I’m really happy to
be a part of.
Tell us about your workshop/studio
I work out of a two-car garage in my parent’s
house. I’m fortunate to have enough space for flat
woodworking machines as well as my lathe. I’ve
got a Nova Orion 18 x 36 lathe that does what I
need it to and basic milling tools.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
I do a lot of both faceplate and spindle turning, so I
like to use the traditional tools associated with
each. For faceplate turning, I like to use a pair of
5/8” bowl gouges, one with a 45 degree swept
back grind and the other with a slightly swept back
65 degree grind whenever possible. I’ll switch to ½”
bowl gouges ground similarly on smaller work. I
also love my Sorby heavy traditional bowl scraper.
For spindle turning, I prefer a heavy roughing
gouge, 1” and ½” skews, a ½” spindle gouge and a
3/8” detail gouge.
What is your favourite wood?
I’ve never been fond of choosing favourites. Here
are a few of the ones I’ve enjoyed working so far:
•
Hard maple: Consistently available and fairly
stable, it makes for a great staple wood that I
always seem to have on hand.
•
London Plane: It moves a lot and can be a pain
to source (since there aren’t too many big ones
that come down locally), but I love its soft pink
(Continued from page 11)
(Continued on page 13)
Some drying blanks
My workbench
Driveway Wood (thanks Dan)

November 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
colour and interlocking grain pattern.
•
Black Locust: It can be a pain to work
(especially with the silicate deposits necessitating near constant tool sharpening), but I love
its shiny golden colour and how nicely it ebonizes due to its high tannin content.
What finishes do you prefer using?
I’m still experimenting with different oils, films etc.
(and testing the long term durability of many) but
my favourites so far are tung oil, shellac and linseed oil finishes. I’m still searching for a good finish
for vessels meant to contain hot liquids for extended periods of time.
Do you ever incorporate other materials into
your pieces?
Sometimes, mostly for necessity and functionality. I
use paints and stains on occasion, but I’d like to
gain more competence with wood as a medium
before adding too many other things. I’m looking
to start adding in human hair and animal bones
etc. to wood art at some point, but I haven’t got to
it yet.
What other types of woodworking or pursuits
do you have?
I do some flat woodworking, though mostly out of
necessity or for friends. I also enjoy playing music,
hairdressing and cooking.
What inspires you - where do you get your
ideas from?
I get a lot of ideas from the internet through social
media and research. That said, the best inspiration
has come from bouncing ideas around with others
and noticing interesting shapes and designs in the
mundane things around me - from oddly curled
potato chips to broken dishware in restaurants.
The wonder and majesty of nature tends to inspire
me as well.
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
In terms of woodturning technique and how I
work, the people in the guild who have mentored
and taught me have been a big influence. As for

Where do you usually display and/or sell your
work?
I’m slowly starting to get my pieces out there. So
far, my work is being carried year-round at Place
des Arts in Coquitlam, and I've recently started
vending at local markets like New West Craft.
Favourite project to date?
I often judge how good a piece is based on how
much I want to keep it for myself. It rarely happens, but I feel that some were made well enough
for me to use them as references for future works.
Pieces like the blue bird kuksa mug and rotund
cherry cup are examples. I like looking at them and
holding them. They also serve as reminders of a
job well done.
Where do you see your work going in future?
I hope to have my work in local artisan shops, consignment stores and at craft fairs/markets. In less
literal terms, I’d like to design and develop unique
products that are utilitarian while being aesthetically pleasing. I’m not sure what all of them will be
yet, but I’ll definitely share once I come up with
them!
Are there any new techniques you would like
to try?
Yes, my profile would be too long if I listed them
all. I’m interested in learning more about therming,
end grain turning, steam bending, metal spinning,
toolmaking and altering, the entire skillset taught
by the Japanese woodturning school in Yamanaka,
urushi finishing, proper hollow forming and so
much more. I’ve yet to fully master even the basic
techniques of woodturning and woodworking in
general, and I’m excited about the possibilities before me.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 28)

November 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 28
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
